q: Expected inflation rises from 2 percent to 5 percent while unemployment remains at its natural rate. Which long-run outcome fits the vertical Phillips curve?
correctAnswer: Inflation is higher, but unemployment is unchanged at the natural rate.
distractors: Inflation is higher and unemployment is permanently lower.
Inflation is unchanged and unemployment falls to zero.
Both inflation and unemployment are permanently higher.
commonError: Treating a higher expected inflation rate as a permanent way to lower unemployment.
feedback: Along the long-run Phillips curve, different inflation rates can coexist with the same natural rate of unemployment.
options: Inflation is higher, but unemployment is unchanged at the natural rate.
Inflation is higher and unemployment is permanently lower.
Inflation is unchanged and unemployment falls to zero.
Both inflation and unemployment are permanently higher.

q: Policymakers repeatedly expand aggregate demand to keep unemployment below its natural rate. Once workers and firms adjust expectations, what is required to keep unemployment below that rate?
correctAnswer: Ever-larger inflation surprises.
distractors: A permanently fixed inflation rate.
A lower natural rate without any labor-market change.
A one-time reduction in expected inflation.
commonError: Assuming one expansion can hold unemployment below the natural rate forever.
feedback: After expectations catch up, only new inflation surprises can again push unemployment temporarily below its natural rate.
options: A permanently fixed inflation rate.
Ever-larger inflation surprises.
A lower natural rate without any labor-market change.
A one-time reduction in expected inflation.

q: Two economies have the same natural unemployment rate but very different average inflation rates over many years. Which observation is most consistent with a vertical long-run Phillips curve?
correctAnswer: Both can remain at the same long-run unemployment rate despite different inflation rates.
distractors: The higher-inflation economy must have permanently lower unemployment because inflation buys a lasting tradeoff.
The lower-inflation economy must have permanently higher unemployment because prices grow more slowly.
Different inflation rates require different natural unemployment rates even when labor markets are otherwise alike.
commonError: Inferring a permanent inflation-unemployment tradeoff from cross-country inflation differences.
feedback: The vertical LRPC allows different steady inflation rates at the same natural unemployment rate.
options: The higher-inflation economy must have permanently lower unemployment because inflation buys a lasting tradeoff.
The lower-inflation economy must have permanently higher unemployment because prices grow more slowly.
Both can remain at the same long-run unemployment rate despite different inflation rates.
Different inflation rates require different natural unemployment rates even when labor markets are otherwise alike.

q: A national job-matching system reduces the time workers spend searching for suitable positions. What happens to the long-run Phillips curve, other things equal?
correctAnswer: It shifts left because the natural rate of unemployment falls.
distractors: It shifts right because expected inflation rises.
The economy moves upward along an unchanged LRPC.
It becomes horizontal at the new inflation rate.
commonError: Confusing a change in the natural rate with a movement caused by inflation.
feedback: A lasting improvement in labor-market matching can lower the natural rate and move the entire LRPC left.
options: It shifts right because expected inflation rises.
The economy moves upward along an unchanged LRPC.
It becomes horizontal at the new inflation rate.
It shifts left because the natural rate of unemployment falls.

q: An unexpected monetary expansion temporarily lowers unemployment. Inflation expectations then fully adjust while the higher inflation rate persists. What is the long-run result?
correctAnswer: Unemployment returns to the natural rate at a higher inflation rate.
distractors: Unemployment remains permanently below the natural rate.
Unemployment rises permanently above the natural rate.
Inflation returns automatically to its original rate while unemployment stays low.
commonError: Stopping the analysis before expectations adjust.
feedback: The short-run unemployment effect disappears when expectations adjust, leaving higher inflation and natural-rate unemployment.
options: Unemployment returns to the natural rate at a higher inflation rate.
Unemployment remains permanently below the natural rate.
Unemployment rises permanently above the natural rate.
Inflation returns automatically to its original rate while unemployment stays low.

q: A government insists on holding unemployment below the natural rate after inflation expectations have adjusted. What does the long-run Phillips-curve model predict?
correctAnswer: The policy requires continuously accelerating inflation.
distractors: A stable inflation rate will permanently sustain lower unemployment.
Unemployment will fall to zero without further inflation.
The natural rate automatically falls whenever aggregate demand rises.
commonError: Believing a stable higher inflation rate buys a permanent unemployment reduction.
feedback: Once expected inflation catches up, maintaining below-natural unemployment requires repeated new inflation surprises.
options: A stable inflation rate will permanently sustain lower unemployment.
The policy requires continuously accelerating inflation.
Unemployment will fall to zero without further inflation.
The natural rate automatically falls whenever aggregate demand rises.

q: Disinflation means that:
correctAnswer: Inflation is slowing, although the price level may still be rising.
distractors: The overall price level is falling because average prices are declining.
Unemployment is falling even though output remains below potential.
Nominal wages are fixed while real wages rise automatically.
commonError: Confusing disinflation with deflation.
feedback: Disinflation is slower price growth; deflation is a falling price level.
options: The overall price level is falling because average prices are declining.
Unemployment is falling even though output remains below potential.
Inflation is slowing, although the price level may still be rising.
Nominal wages are fixed while real wages rise automatically.

q: Why can a credible anti-inflation announcement reduce the short-run cost of disinflation?
correctAnswer: Expected inflation may adjust downward more quickly.
distractors: It permanently eliminates the natural rate of unemployment.
It guarantees that the price level falls immediately.
It makes aggregate demand irrelevant.
commonError: Ignoring the role of expected inflation in the transition.
feedback: When expectations fall sooner, wage and price setting can adjust with less output and unemployment loss.
options: It permanently eliminates the natural rate of unemployment.
It guarantees that the price level falls immediately.
It makes aggregate demand irrelevant.
Expected inflation may adjust downward more quickly.

q: The sacrifice ratio measures the:
correctAnswer: Cumulative output lost per percentage-point reduction in inflation.
distractors: The permanent unemployment rate created by a recession.
The price-level increase caused by one point of money growth.
The share of public spending financed by current taxes.
commonError: Treating the sacrifice ratio as a permanent unemployment rate.
feedback: The sacrifice ratio summarizes the output cost of lowering inflation.
options: Cumulative output lost per percentage-point reduction in inflation.
The permanent unemployment rate created by a recession.
The price-level increase caused by one point of money growth.
The share of public spending financed by current taxes.

q: A central bank announces a gradual disinflation, but households and firms doubt that the plan will continue. What is the most likely consequence?
correctAnswer: High expected inflation can prolong the output and job losses.
distractors: The natural unemployment rate immediately falls to zero.
The price level must begin falling throughout the adjustment.
Unemployment cannot rise because the disinflation is gradual.
commonError: Assuming gradualism automatically produces low transition costs.
feedback: If the plan lacks credibility, expected inflation can adjust slowly and make the disinflation more costly.
options: The natural unemployment rate immediately falls to zero.
High expected inflation can prolong the output and job losses.
The price level must begin falling throughout the adjustment.
Unemployment cannot rise because the disinflation is gradual.

q: Country A has a sacrifice ratio of 2, while Country B has a sacrifice ratio of 5. If both reduce inflation by 3 percentage points, which comparison is correct?
correctAnswer: A loses about 6% of annual GDP cumulatively; B loses about 15%.
distractors: A loses about 15% of annual GDP cumulatively; B loses about 6%.
Both lose about 3% of annual GDP because the inflation reduction is equal.
A has no output loss because its sacrifice ratio is below the inflation reduction.
commonError: Reversing the sacrifice ratios or treating equal inflation reductions as equal output costs.
feedback: Cumulative output loss equals the sacrifice ratio times the inflation reduction: 2 × 3 = 6 for A and 5 × 3 = 15 for B.
options: A loses about 15% of annual GDP cumulatively; B loses about 6%.
Both lose about 3% of annual GDP because the inflation reduction is equal.
A loses about 6% of annual GDP cumulatively; B loses about 15%.
A has no output loss because its sacrifice ratio is below the inflation reduction.

q: Two central banks pursue the same reduction in inflation. One has strong credibility and expected inflation falls quickly. Compared with the less credible bank, what is the likely transition?
correctAnswer: A smaller temporary output and unemployment cost.
distractors: A permanently lower natural rate of unemployment.
A larger price-level increase caused by credibility.
No change in expected inflation.
commonError: Assuming credibility changes the long-run natural rate rather than the transition cost.
feedback: Faster adjustment of expected inflation can reduce the sacrifice required to lower actual inflation.
options: A permanently lower natural rate of unemployment.
A larger price-level increase caused by credibility.
No change in expected inflation.
A smaller temporary output and unemployment cost.

q: Which unemployment is excluded from the natural rate?
correctAnswer: Cyclical unemployment caused by a recessionary gap.
distractors: Frictional unemployment from job search.
Structural unemployment from skill mismatch.
Unemployment caused by normal worker turnover.
commonError: Including cyclical unemployment in the natural-rate baseline.
feedback: The natural rate includes frictional and structural unemployment, not recession-driven cyclical unemployment.
options: Cyclical unemployment caused by a recessionary gap.
Frictional unemployment from job search.
Structural unemployment from skill mismatch.
Unemployment caused by normal worker turnover.

q: The natural rate of unemployment is best described as:
correctAnswer: A normal benchmark that can change as labor-market conditions change.
distractors: A fixed constant that must be identical in every decade.
A target of zero unemployment.
The unemployment rate observed only during recessions.
commonError: Treating the natural rate as zero or permanently fixed.
feedback: Demographics, institutions, matching efficiency, and structural change can alter the natural rate.
options: A fixed constant that must be identical in every decade.
A normal benchmark that can change as labor-market conditions change.
A target of zero unemployment.
The unemployment rate observed only during recessions.

q: A more effective job-search platform helps workers find suitable jobs faster. What is the most likely effect on the natural rate?
correctAnswer: It falls because frictional unemployment is reduced.
distractors: It rises because cyclical unemployment increases.
It becomes equal to the inflation rate.
It cannot change because the natural rate is fixed.
commonError: Assuming better matching affects only cyclical unemployment.
feedback: Faster matching shortens normal job search and can lower the natural rate.
options: It rises because cyclical unemployment increases.
It becomes equal to the inflation rate.
It falls because frictional unemployment is reduced.
It cannot change because the natural rate is fixed.

q: A rapid shift away from coal production leaves many workers without the skills demanded by expanding industries. What is the most likely effect?
correctAnswer: Structural unemployment and the natural rate may rise.
distractors: Cyclical unemployment must fall to zero.
The natural rate must fall because jobs changed.
Frictional unemployment disappears immediately.
commonError: Classifying a persistent skill mismatch as only cyclical unemployment.
feedback: Sectoral change can raise structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.
options: Cyclical unemployment must fall to zero.
The natural rate must fall because jobs changed.
Frictional unemployment disappears immediately.
Structural unemployment and the natural rate may rise.

q: Actual unemployment is below the estimated natural rate. Which interpretation is strongest?
correctAnswer: The labor market is unusually tight, with possible inflation pressure.
distractors: The economy has eliminated every form of unemployment.
Structural unemployment must have fallen permanently to zero.
The economy must be operating with a recessionary output gap.
commonError: Equating below-natural unemployment with zero unemployment or recession.
feedback: Unemployment below the natural rate indicates a tight labor market, not the disappearance of frictional and structural unemployment.
options: The labor market is unusually tight, with possible inflation pressure.
The economy has eliminated every form of unemployment.
Structural unemployment must have fallen permanently to zero.
The economy must be operating with a recessionary output gap.

q: A temporary collapse in aggregate demand ends, and spending returns to normal. What should happen to unemployment if the natural rate itself did not change?
correctAnswer: Cyclical unemployment fades, moving actual unemployment toward the natural rate.
distractors: The natural rate rises permanently by the recession increase.
Frictional unemployment falls permanently to zero after spending recovers.
Actual unemployment remains at its recession peak even after demand returns.
commonError: Treating a temporary demand-driven unemployment increase as a permanent natural-rate shift.
feedback: When the demand shortfall closes, cyclical unemployment recedes and the unemployment rate moves toward its natural benchmark.
options: The natural rate rises permanently by the recession increase.
Cyclical unemployment fades, moving actual unemployment toward the natural rate.
Frictional unemployment falls permanently to zero after spending recovers.
Actual unemployment remains at its recession peak even after demand returns.

q: A long recession causes workers to lose skills and attachment to the labor force. Why might unemployment remain elevated after aggregate demand recovers?
correctAnswer: Hysteresis may have raised the natural rate through lasting labor-market damage.
distractors: The natural rate must remain unchanged after every recession.
Cyclical unemployment automatically becomes permanent inflation.
Frictional unemployment can exist only while the economy is expanding.
commonError: Assuming all recession unemployment disappears without lasting effects.
feedback: A prolonged downturn can create persistent skill loss or detachment that raises structural unemployment and the natural rate.
options: The natural rate must remain unchanged after every recession.
Cyclical unemployment automatically becomes permanent inflation.
Hysteresis may have raised the natural rate through lasting labor-market damage.
Frictional unemployment can exist only while the economy is expanding.

q: Which statement corrects the claim that the natural rate is always zero and never changes?
correctAnswer: It is normally positive and can change with labor-market conditions.
distractors: It always equals cyclical unemployment in the current year.
It is permanently fixed by the central bank’s inflation target.
It includes only people who have completely stopped seeking work.
commonError: Treating the natural rate as zero and immutable.
feedback: The natural rate reflects normal search and mismatch, and its level can change over time.
options: It always equals cyclical unemployment in the current year.
It is permanently fixed by the central bank’s inflation target.
It includes only people who have completely stopped seeking work.
It is normally positive and can change with labor-market conditions.

q: A pension has a full cost-of-living adjustment tied to the CPI. If measured inflation is 4 percent, what is the intended effect?
correctAnswer: Raise the nominal payment about 4% to protect purchasing power.
distractors: Reduce the nominal payment about 4% to offset inflation.
Hold the nominal payment fixed so its real value automatically rises.
Convert the pension payment into a market interest rate.
commonError: Confusing nominal indexation with a reduction in benefits.
feedback: A CPI-linked adjustment raises the nominal amount to offset measured price growth.
options: Raise the nominal payment about 4% to protect purchasing power.
Reduce the nominal payment about 4% to offset inflation.
Hold the nominal payment fixed so its real value automatically rises.
Convert the pension payment into a market interest rate.

q: Suppose the CPI systematically overstates the rise in the true cost of living. What can happen to a benefit that is fully indexed to the CPI?
correctAnswer: The benefit can become too generous in real terms.
distractors: The nominal benefit must decline every year.
The real value remains exactly constant by definition.
Indexing removes every possible measurement problem.
commonError: Assuming an index-linked adjustment is exact even when the index is biased.
feedback: If the CPI overstates cost-of-living growth, full CPI indexation can overcompensate recipients in real terms.
options: The nominal benefit must decline every year.
The benefit can become too generous in real terms.
The real value remains exactly constant by definition.
Indexing removes every possible measurement problem.

q: Which distinction between the Federal Reserve and the U.S. Treasury is correct?
correctAnswer: The Fed conducts monetary policy, while the Treasury manages federal finances and debt operations.
distractors: The Treasury sets the federal funds rate, while the Fed writes tax laws.
The Fed passes the federal budget, while the Treasury regulates inflation expectations.
Both institutions perform exactly the same functions.
commonError: Treating the central bank and fiscal authority as the same institution.
feedback: The Fed is the monetary authority; the Treasury is part of the executive branch and manages federal finances.
options: The Treasury sets the federal funds rate, while the Fed writes tax laws.
The Fed passes the federal budget, while the Treasury regulates inflation expectations.
The Fed conducts monetary policy, while the Treasury manages federal finances and debt operations.
Both institutions perform exactly the same functions.

q: During a panic, a solvent bank cannot obtain short-term funding even though its assets exceed its liabilities. What central-bank response best fits the lender-of-last-resort role?
correctAnswer: Provide temporary liquidity against sound collateral.
distractors: Guarantee every bank loss without conditions.
Finance a permanent tax cut.
Raise reserve requirements solely to remove liquidity.
commonError: Confusing liquidity support with an unconditional bailout of insolvent institutions.
feedback: Lender-of-last-resort support addresses temporary liquidity problems while safeguards limit losses and moral hazard.
options: Guarantee every bank loss without conditions.
Finance a permanent tax cut.
Raise reserve requirements solely to remove liquidity.
Provide temporary liquidity against sound collateral.

q: Which institutional arrangement best combines central-bank independence with democratic accountability?
correctAnswer: Public officials set the mandate; the central bank chooses instruments and reports transparently.
distractors: The central bank chooses national goals and never explains its decisions to the public.
Elected officials directly set policy interest rates before every national election.
The Treasury secretly directs monetary operations without a published mandate.
commonError: Treating independence as freedom from any public mandate or oversight.
feedback: Instrument independence can coexist with a legislated mandate, transparency, and public accountability.
options: Public officials set the mandate; the central bank chooses instruments and reports transparently.
The central bank chooses national goals and never explains its decisions to the public.
Elected officials directly set policy interest rates before every national election.
The Treasury secretly directs monetary operations without a published mandate.

q: When the central bank buys a large quantity of longer-term securities, what happens directly on its balance sheet?
correctAnswer: Its securities assets and reserve liabilities usually both rise.
distractors: Tax revenue rises while currency liabilities disappear from the balance sheet.
Government purchases of goods rise automatically with the securities purchase.
Commercial-bank capital is converted directly into federal tax receipts.
commonError: Treating asset purchases as ordinary fiscal spending.
feedback: A central-bank asset purchase expands its asset holdings and typically creates reserve liabilities.
options: Tax revenue rises while currency liabilities disappear from the balance sheet.
Its securities assets and reserve liabilities usually both rise.
Government purchases of goods rise automatically with the securities purchase.
Commercial-bank capital is converted directly into federal tax receipts.

q: The short-term policy rate is near its effective lower bound. Which action is still a monetary-policy option?
correctAnswer: Use forward guidance or buy longer-term securities.
distractors: Change federal income-tax rates through the banking system.
Authorize a new congressional spending program immediately.
Set private-sector wages and prices by administrative order.
commonError: Assuming monetary policy has no remaining tools when a short-term rate is very low.
feedback: Central banks may use communication and balance-sheet tools when conventional rate cuts are constrained.
options: Change federal income-tax rates through the banking system.
Authorize a new congressional spending program immediately.
Use forward guidance or buy longer-term securities.
Set private-sector wages and prices by administrative order.

q: A government persistently pressures its central bank to create money to finance large deficits. What institutional risk is most relevant?
correctAnswer: Fiscal dominance can weaken price stability and central-bank credibility.
distractors: The natural rate of unemployment automatically becomes zero.
The money supply becomes unrelated to the central bank.
Budget deficits cease to have opportunity costs.
commonError: Ignoring how fiscal pressure can compromise monetary-policy objectives.
feedback: Under fiscal dominance, debt-financing pressure can subordinate monetary policy and raise inflation risk.
options: The natural rate of unemployment automatically becomes zero.
The money supply becomes unrelated to the central bank.
Budget deficits cease to have opportunity costs.
Fiscal dominance can weaken price stability and central-bank credibility.

q: Emergency lending stops a bank run, but banks now expect rescue whenever they take large risks. What tradeoff does the central bank face?
correctAnswer: Financial stability today versus greater moral hazard tomorrow.
distractors: Lower inflation today versus a permanently lower natural rate.
Higher taxes today versus lower government spending tomorrow.
More exports today versus fewer imports tomorrow.
commonError: Evaluating emergency lending without considering future risk-taking incentives.
feedback: Liquidity support can stabilize the system, but poorly designed guarantees can encourage excessive risk.
options: Financial stability today versus greater moral hazard tomorrow.
Lower inflation today versus a permanently lower natural rate.
Higher taxes today versus lower government spending tomorrow.
More exports today versus fewer imports tomorrow.

q: Why does central-bank independence not mean the central bank should be free to choose any social objective it wants?
correctAnswer: Independence covers instrument choice within a publicly established mandate.
distractors: Independence requires all monetary-policy decisions to remain secret.
The central bank must directly control federal taxes and spending.
Independence means elected institutions have no legitimate policy role.
commonError: Equating instrument independence with unlimited policy authority.
feedback: A legitimate framework separates public goal setting from day-to-day instrument choices and requires accountability.
options: Independence requires all monetary-policy decisions to remain secret.
Independence covers instrument choice within a publicly established mandate.
The central bank must directly control federal taxes and spending.
Independence means elected institutions have no legitimate policy role.

q: Inflation is well above target and output is near potential, but elected officials demand easier money before an election. What is the strongest case for central-bank independence?
correctAnswer: It resists election-driven easing and protects price-stability credibility.
distractors: It guarantees that monetary tightening has no short-run output cost.
It allows the central bank to eliminate every federal budget deficit.
It permanently fixes unemployment below the natural rate.
commonError: Assuming independence removes policy tradeoffs rather than improving commitment.
feedback: Independence can support credible commitment to price stability even when near-term political incentives favor expansion.
options: It guarantees that monetary tightening has no short-run output cost.
It allows the central bank to eliminate every federal budget deficit.
It resists election-driven easing and protects price-stability credibility.
It permanently fixes unemployment below the natural rate.

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes ex ante and ex post real interest rates?
correctAnswer: Ex ante uses expected inflation; ex post uses actual inflation.
distractors: Both measures subtract actual inflation from the nominal rate.
Ex ante adds expected inflation to the nominal interest rate.
Ex post is known with certainty when the loan contract is signed.
commonError: Using actual inflation for both the expected and realized real return.
feedback: The expected real return is based on expected inflation, while the realized real return uses actual inflation.
options: Both measures subtract actual inflation from the nominal rate.
Ex ante adds expected inflation to the nominal interest rate.
Ex post is known with certainty when the loan contract is signed.
Ex ante uses expected inflation; ex post uses actual inflation.

q: A temporary negative aggregate-demand shock lowers output below potential. With no policy response and flexible wages and expected prices over time, what is the long-run outcome?
correctAnswer: SRAS shifts right and output returns to potential at a lower price level.
distractors: Output remains permanently below potential with the original price level.
LRAS shifts left until productive capacity matches the recession output.
Aggregate demand automatically shifts right because unemployment increased.
commonError: Treating a temporary demand shock as a permanent change in productive capacity.
feedback: Falling wages and expected prices shift SRAS right, restoring natural output while leaving the price level lower.
options: SRAS shifts right and output returns to potential at a lower price level.
Output remains permanently below potential with the original price level.
LRAS shifts left until productive capacity matches the recession output.
Aggregate demand automatically shifts right because unemployment increased.

q: In the long-run AD–AS model, natural output is determined mainly by:
correctAnswer: Labor, capital, natural resources, technology, and institutions.
distractors: The current price level alone.
The latest movement in aggregate demand alone.
The nominal money supply with no real-side conditions.
commonError: Treating natural output as a price-level or demand choice.
feedback: Natural output reflects the economy’s productive capacity and real institutions.
options: The current price level alone.
Labor, capital, natural resources, technology, and institutions.
The latest movement in aggregate demand alone.
The nominal money supply with no real-side conditions.

q: An economy has a recessionary gap and policymakers do nothing. Which self-correcting sequence is most consistent with the model?
correctAnswer: Lower wage and price expectations shift SRAS right toward potential.
distractors: Higher wages shift SRAS left and deepen the recessionary gap.
LRAS shifts left until potential output equals the depressed output level.
Aggregate demand rises automatically because the current price level is fixed.
commonError: Reversing the wage and SRAS adjustment in a recessionary gap.
feedback: Below-potential output puts downward pressure on wages and expected prices, allowing SRAS to shift right.
options: Higher wages shift SRAS left and deepen the recessionary gap.
LRAS shifts left until potential output equals the depressed output level.
Lower wage and price expectations shift SRAS right toward potential.
Aggregate demand rises automatically because the current price level is fixed.

q: Demand growth pushes output above potential. If no stabilization policy is used, which long-run adjustment is most likely?
correctAnswer: Rising costs shift SRAS left, returning output to potential at a higher price level.
distractors: Falling wages shift SRAS right and push output farther above potential.
LRAS shifts right solely because the current price level has increased.
Output stays permanently above potential without creating inflation pressure.
commonError: Using recessionary-gap adjustment for an inflationary gap.
feedback: An overheated labor market raises costs and expected prices, shifting SRAS left and closing the inflationary gap.
options: Falling wages shift SRAS right and push output farther above potential.
LRAS shifts right solely because the current price level has increased.
Output stays permanently above potential without creating inflation pressure.
Rising costs shift SRAS left, returning output to potential at a higher price level.
